title: Regression Algorithms
summary: Regression predicts continuous values - like prices, temperatures, or scores. Linear regression is the foundational algorithm and a great way to understand how models fit data by minimizing error. Regularization techniques like Ridge and Lasso preven
content:
# Regression Algorithms ##### The model that priced a house at negative ₹40 lakh A student built a house-price model with 180 features on a dataset of 400 homes. Training R² was 0.998 — almost perfect. On new data it produced predictions ranging from ₹−40 lakh to ₹19 crore for ordinary three-bedroom flats. The problem was that 180 features and 400 samples means the model has enough freedom to fit the training data exactly, including its noise. Several features were also nearly duplicates — `carpet_area`, `built_up_area` and `super_built_up_area` are all roughly proportional to each other. When features are that correlated, the model cannot determine which one matters, and it compensates by assigning enormous coefficients that cancel out on training data and explode on anything else. Both problems have the same fix, and it is one of the most useful ideas in applied ML: **regularization**. Understanding regression properly — including its assumptions and failure modes — is what makes the rest of supervised learning make sense, because linear regression is the simplest model where every important concept already appears. ##### Linear regression Linear regression fits a straight line (or hyperplane) through the data: ```text ŷ = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + ... + wₙxₙ + b ``` The `w` values are **coefficients** — how much the prediction changes per unit change in that feature. `b` is the **intercept**, the prediction when all features are zero. Training means finding the coefficients that minimize mean squared error. Unlike most models, linear regression has a **closed-form solution** — you can compute the answer directly rather than iterating: ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score rng = np.random.default_rng(42) n = 500 area = rng.uniform(500, 3000, n) bedrooms = rng.integers(1, 5, n) age = rng.uniform(0, 40, n) price = 4500 * area + 300_000 * bedrooms - 25_000 * age + rng.normal(0, 400_000, n) X = np.column_stack([area, bedrooms, age]) X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, price, test_size=0.2, random_state=42) model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train) for name, coef in zip(["area", "bedrooms", "age"], model.coef_): print(f"{name:>9}: {coef:>12,.0f}") print(f"intercept: {model.intercept_:>12,.0f}") ``` The coefficients are the reason linear regression remains valuable despite being the simplest option: they are **directly interpretable**. A coefficient of 4,500 on area means each additional square foot adds ₹4,500 to the predicted price, holding other features constant. Very few models offer that clarity, and in regulated domains — lending, insurance, healthcare — interpretability is often a requirement rather than a preference. ##### Regression metrics Four metrics, each answering a different question: ```python y_pred = model.predict(X_test) mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred) mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred) rmse = np.sqrt(mse) r2 = r2_score(y_test, y_pred) print(f"MAE {mae:>14,.0f}") # average absolute error, in rupees print(f"RMSE {rmse:>14,.0f}") # penalizes large errors, in rupees print(f"R² {r2:>14.4f}") # proportion of variance explained ``` | Metric | Meaning | Use when | |---|---|---| | **MAE** | Mean absolute error, in original units | You want a plain "typically off by X" | | **MSE** | Mean squared error | Optimization (differentiable everywhere) | | **RMSE** | √MSE, in original units | Large errors are disproportionately costly | | **R²** | Fraction of variance explained (0–1) | Comparing across datasets | The distinction that matters in practice: **RMSE penalizes large errors far more than MAE.** Being wrong by ₹10 lakh once contributes more to RMSE than being wrong by ₹1 lakh ten times. Choose RMSE when big mistakes are especially bad; choose MAE when all errors are equally undesirable and outliers should not dominate. **R² can be negative.** It compares your model to simply predicting the mean — a negative value means you are worse than that. The overfit house-price model would have scored negative on test data. Note also that R² always increases when you add features, even useless ones, which is why **adjusted R²** exists and why you should judge on a held-out set rather than on training R². ##### Polynomial regression When the relationship curves, add polynomial terms. The model stays *linear in its coefficients* — which is why it is still "linear regression" — but can fit curves: ```python from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline for degree in (1, 3, 15): poly_model = make_pipeline( PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False), StandardScaler(), LinearRegression(), ).fit(X_train, y_train) print(f"degree {degree:>2}: train R² {poly_model.score(X_train, y_train):>6.3f} " f"test R² {poly_model.score(X_test, y_test):>8.3f}") ``` Two cautions. **Feature count explodes**: degree 3 on 10 features produces 285 terms, degree 5 produces over 3,000. And **high degrees overfit spectacularly** — degree 15 will fit the training data closely and oscillate wildly between points. Note the `StandardScaler` in the pipeline. Polynomial features have wildly different scales (`area` versus `area³`), and without scaling the numerical conditioning becomes terrible. ##### Ridge and Lasso regularization Regularization adds a penalty for large coefficients, forcing the model to justify complexity. This is the fix for both problems in the opening story. **Ridge (L2)** adds the sum of *squared* coefficients to the loss: ```text Loss = MSE + α · Σ wᵢ² ``` **Lasso (L1)** adds the sum of *absolute* coefficients: ```text Loss = MSE + α · Σ |wᵢ| ``` That difference in the penalty produces a genuinely different behaviour, and it is the assignment's question: ```python from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet, LinearRegression # 30 features, only 5 of which actually matter n, p = 200, 30 X = rng.normal(size=(n, p)) true_w = np.zeros(p) true_w[:5] = [3.0, -2.0, 1.5, 4.0, -1.0] y = X @ true_w + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n) Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42) for name, m in [("OLS", LinearRegression()), ("Ridge α=1", Ridge(alpha=1.0)), ("Lasso α=0.1", Lasso(alpha=0.1))]: m.fit(Xtr, ytr) zeros = int(np.sum(np.abs(m.coef_) < 1e-6)) print(f"{name:<12} test R² {m.score(Xte, yte):.3f} " f"max|coef| {np.abs(m.coef_).max():>5.2f} exact zeros: {zeros}/{p}") # OLS test R² 0.941 max|coef| 4.13 exact zeros: 0/30 # Ridge α=1 test R² 0.952 max|coef| 3.71 exact zeros: 0/30 # Lasso α=0.1 test R² 0.961 max|coef| 3.92 exact zeros: 22/30 ``` **Ridge shrinks all coefficients toward zero but never exactly to zero.** It keeps every feature, just with reduced influence. Ideal when many features each contribute a little, and particularly good at handling correlated features — it spreads the coefficient across them rather than picking arbitrarily. **Lasso drives some coefficients to exactly zero**, performing automatic feature selection (Tibshirani, 1996). Ideal when you believe most features are irrelevant and you want a sparse, interpretable model. With correlated features it tends to pick one and zero the others, which can be arbitrary. **ElasticNet** combines both, giving you sparsity while handling correlated groups more gracefully: ```python ElasticNet(alpha=0.1, l1_ratio=0.5) # l1_ratio: 0 = pure Ridge, 1 = pure Lasso ``` Choosing `alpha` is not guesswork — use cross-validation: ```python from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV, LassoCV ridge_cv = RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 50)).fit(Xtr, ytr) lasso_cv = LassoCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 1, 50), cv=5, max_iter=5000).fit(Xtr, ytr) print(f"best ridge α: {ridge_cv.alpha_:.4f} best lasso α: {lasso_cv.alpha_:.4f}") ``` **Regularization requires scaled features.** The penalty applies to coefficient magnitudes, and a feature measured in rupees will have a tiny coefficient while one measured in fractions has a large one — so the penalty would fall unequally on them for reasons having nothing to do with importance. Always put a `StandardScaler` before a regularized model. ##### Assumptions of linear regression Linear regression makes five assumptions. When they are violated, coefficients and confidence intervals become unreliable — even if predictions look acceptable. 1. **Linearity** — the relationship is actually linear. Check with a residual plot. 2. **Independence** — observations do not influence each other. Time series violate this. 3. **Homoscedasticity** — residual variance is constant across the prediction range. 4. **Normality of residuals** — errors are roughly normally distributed. Matters for inference, less for prediction. 5. **No perfect multicollinearity** — features are not exact linear combinations of each other. **The residual plot is the diagnostic that checks three of these at once:** ```python import matplotlib.pyplot as plt residuals = y_test - y_pred fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4)) axes[0].scatter(y_pred, residuals, alpha=0.5) axes[0].axhline(0, color="crimson", linestyle="--") axes[0].set_xlabel("Predicted"); axes[0].set_ylabel("Residual") axes[0].set_title("Residuals vs fitted") from scipy import stats stats.probplot(residuals, dist="norm", plot=axes[1]) axes[1].set_title("Q-Q plot of residuals") fig.tight_layout() ``` What to look for: residuals should be a **structureless cloud centred on zero**. A curved pattern means the relationship is nonlinear (add polynomial terms). A funnel shape — spreading out as predictions grow — means heteroscedasticity, usually fixed by log-transforming the target. Points far from the line on the Q-Q plot indicate non-normal residuals. Plotting residuals takes one minute and catches problems no summary metric reveals. ##### Multicollinearity When features are highly correlated, the model cannot separate their individual effects. Coefficients become unstable — large, sometimes with the wrong sign, and swinging wildly if you retrain on a slightly different sample. This is the second failure in the opening story. Detect it with the **Variance Inflation Factor**: ```python from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor import pandas as pd def vif_report(X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame: return pd.DataFrame({ "feature": X.columns, "VIF": [variance_inflation_factor(X.values, i) for i in range(X.shape[1])], }).sort_values("VIF", ascending=False) # VIF interpretation: # 1 = no correlation with other features # 1-5 = moderate, generally fine # 5-10 = high, investigate # > 10 = severe multicollinearity ``` The remedies: **drop one** of a correlated pair; **combine them** into a single feature (a ratio or an average); **use Ridge**, which handles correlated features gracefully by design; or **apply PCA** to produce uncorrelated components at the cost of interpretability. Importantly, multicollinearity harms *coefficient interpretation* far more than *prediction accuracy*. If you only need predictions, it may not matter. If you need to explain which feature drives the outcome, it matters enormously. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Regression problem] --> B[Baseline: predict the mean] B --> C[Linear regression
+ scaled features] C --> D[Plot residuals] D -->|curved pattern| E[Add polynomial terms] D -->|funnel shape| F[Log-transform target] D -->|structureless cloud| G[Check VIF] G -->|VIF > 10| H[Ridge / drop / combine] G -->|VIF fine| I{Train >> test R²?} E --> I F --> I H --> I I -->|yes, overfitting| J[Ridge or Lasso
tune α by CV] I -->|no| K[Report MAE, RMSE, R²
on the test set] J --> K ``` ##### Common mistakes - **Not scaling before regularization**, so the penalty falls arbitrarily. - **Judging on training R²**, which always rises with more features. - **High-degree polynomials** producing wild extrapolation. - **Never plotting residuals** — the cheapest diagnostic available. - **Interpreting coefficients under multicollinearity** as feature importance. - **Extrapolating beyond the training range.** A model trained on 500–3,000 sq ft homes says nothing reliable about a 12,000 sq ft one. - **Using R² alone** without an error metric in real units — stakeholders understand rupees, not variance explained. - **Ignoring heteroscedasticity**, so the model is systematically worse at the high end. - **Random splits on time-ordered data.** - **Reporting more precision than the data supports** — ±₹4 lakh RMSE does not justify predicting to the rupee. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: train **linear, polynomial and Ridge regression** models on a housing dataset and compare **RMSE and R²**. Report both training and test scores for each — the polynomial model will show the widening gap that Ridge then narrows, which demonstrates regularization working rather than merely describing it. The mini project is a **house price prediction model with feature engineering and regularization**, reporting **which features most influence price**. The feature engineering is where the gains are: price per square foot in the locality, age bands, a bathroom-to-bedroom ratio, distance to the city centre. For influence, use standardized coefficients from a Ridge model (raw coefficients are not comparable across differently-scaled features), and state the multicollinearity caveat honestly. For the assignment, **compare Ridge and Lasso**: how each handles coefficients, and when to choose which. Run the sparse-features experiment above yourself and report the count of exact zeros — seeing Lasso zero out 22 of 30 coefficients while Ridge zeroes none is the clearest possible illustration. Then state the selection rule: Ridge when many features each contribute a little or when features are correlated; Lasso when you believe most are irrelevant and want automatic feature selection. ##### Key takeaways - Linear regression's coefficients are directly interpretable, which is why it remains valuable in regulated and explanation-driven contexts. - Report MAE or RMSE alongside R² — errors in original units are what stakeholders can act on, and R² can go negative on a bad model. - Regularization penalizes large coefficients: Ridge shrinks all of them smoothly, Lasso drives some to exactly zero and selects features. - Always scale features before regularizing, and tune `alpha` with cross-validation rather than guessing. - Plot residuals on every regression — a curve means add nonlinearity, a funnel means transform the target, and high VIF means your coefficients are not trustworthy as importances.
